source.title_on_document: Homogenizing effect of large language models (LLMs) on creative diversity: An empirical comparison of human and ChatGPT writing

supplement.holds: Contents described by the main text, not independently inspected: Table S1, regressions with log essay count and authorship dummies only (p. 4, footnote 3); Table S3, pairwise diversity-growth-rate comparisons (pp. 5 and 7); Figs. S1-S3 and Tables S6-S7, Sentence-BERT robustness checks (p. 3, Section 3.4.1); Table S7 is also cited for applicant demographics (p. 3, Section 3.3.1); Table S8, preregistrations (p. 2, Section 3.2); Tables S9-S10, preregistration deviations (pp. 2-3, Section 3.2); Table S10 is also cited for coherence and readability of parameter-modified essays (p. 8, Discussion); essay-length comparisons (p. 3, Section 3.3.2). paper_design_summary: Three preregistered studies analyzed 2,200 college admissions essays, comparing archival essays submitted to a private East Coast university in 2018-2022 with essays generated by GPT-4; Study 2 varied prompts and model parameters, and Study 3 added chain-of-thought prompting and a human group sampled for racial and ethnic diversity (pp. 3, 5, and 7). No human writer was assigned AI assistance. Each essay received a BERT-based Divergent Semantic Integration score, and each condition received a diversity growth rate estimated from collective semantic diversity over pools of 2 to 34 essays (pp. 3-4, Sections 3.4-3.5).

studies.label: Study 1: 100 human vs 100 base GPT-4 admissions essays (GPT-4 through the ChatGPT interface)

assignment.what_was_assigned: No AI assistance was assigned to people. The authors randomly sampled 100 archival human essays and generated 100 essays with GPT-4 through the ChatGPT interface; human authors were not assigned to either condition (p. 5, Section 4.1).
assignment.quote: We compared a set of 100 essays written by humans randomly chosen from submissions between 2018 and 2022 with another set of 100 essays generated using GPT-4.
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 2, Section 3.2 (OSF https://osf.io/ywap5/registrations; Study 1 registered July 5, 2023; deviations for Studies 1 and 2 in Tables S9-S10, supplement)

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 through the ChatGPT chat interface (June 24-30, 2023); the API was not accessible to the authors at the time
ai_tool.how_used: GPT-4 wrote whole essays on its own; no human applicant received AI assistance in the study. Instruction placed ahead of the essay prompt: 'As a college applicant, please generate my admissions essay of approximately 650 words in response to the following prompt: [Essay Prompt].' (p. 3, Section 3.3.2; p. 5, Section 4.1)

task.description: College admissions essay answering: 'As OOOO University is a diverse community, the Admissions Committee would like to know more about you in your words. Please submit a brief essay, either personal or creative, which you feel best describes you.' GPT-4 was asked for about 650 words, the average length of the human essays (p. 3).

outcomes.name: Individual diversity (Divergent Semantic Integration, DSI) of each essay
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: DSI (Johnson et al., 2022): mean cosine distance between all pairs of word embeddings within one essay, from bert-large-uncased layers 6 and 7, multiplied by 1,000. The paper calls it 'individual diversity' and uses it as the creativity level of an essay; higher DSI means greater creativity (pp. 3-4, Sections 3.4.1-3.4.2). Welch t-test (p. 4, Section 3.5). Robustness with Sentence-BERT all-mpnet-base-v2 embeddings, with and without sampling, in Figs. S1-S3 and Tables S6-S7 (supplement, not in this PDF).

contrasts.reported: Table 1, Human minus Base GPT-4: Mean Difference 8.95, 95% CI 7.14, 10.76, Cohen’s d 1.38, t 9.75, p < 0.001 (no correction, one comparison); text: Mean Difference = 8.95, t(159.89) = 9.75, p < .001, Cohen’s d = 1.38 (Welch t-test). Fig. 1: Human 829.59 (7.92), n = 100; Base GPT-4 820.64 (4.64), n = 100 (the parenthesized values are unlabeled; see open_questions).
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section 4.2.1; p. 6, Table 1 and Fig. 1

outcomes.name: Diversity growth rate (DGR) of collective diversity
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Collective diversity: DSI of 34 sentences randomly sampled from k randomly chosen essays of one condition, averaged over 5,000 draws, for k = 2 to 34 (33 scores per condition). DGR: slope b on ln(k) from a regression of collective diversity on ln(k), authorship dummies (human as reference), and their interactions; doubling effect = b x ln(2) (p. 4, Sections 3.4.3 and 3.5). Slope differences tested by post-hoc pairwise comparisons, detailed in Table S3 (supplement). Sentence-BERT robustness in Figs. S1-S3 and Tables S6-S7 (supplement).

contrasts.reported: Table 2: Human DGR b = 0.58, 95% CI 0.50, 0.66, doubling effect 0.40, SE 0.04, df 62, t 15.35, p < 0.001; Base GPT-4 b = 0.18, 95% CI 0.11, 0.26, doubling effect 0.13, SE 0.04, df 62, t 4.82, p < 0.001. Text: slope difference b = 0.40, 95% CI = [0.29, 0.50], p < .001; the base rate is 'only about 31% of the diversity growth rate observed for human-written essays'. No SE or t is printed for the difference.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section 4.2.2; p. 6, Table 2; p. 7, Fig. 2; pairwise detail in Table S3 (supplement)

diversity_detail.metric: Diversity growth rate: slope of collective diversity (mean pairwise cosine distance among BERT word embeddings in 34 sentences sampled from k pooled essays, x 1,000) on ln(k), k = 2 to 34
diversity_detail.computed_over: All word pairs within 34 sentences randomly sampled from k randomly chosen essays of the same condition; 5,000 draws per k, averaged; 33 collective-diversity scores per condition (k = 2 to 34)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Multiple regression of the 33 collective-diversity scores per condition on ln(k), authorship dummies, and their interactions (df 62); per-slope SE, 95% CI, and t; post-hoc pairwise slope comparison. The regression's observations are the averaged pool scores, not essays.
diversity_detail.notes: Higher DGR means each added essay adds more collective diversity (less homogenization), so no sign reversal applies. The comparison is between a pool of applicants' essays and a pool of GPT-4 outputs, not between people who did and did not use AI. n_units 66 = 33 scores x 2 conditions (p. 4; df 62 in Table 2). Fig. 2 plots collective minus individual diversity.

studies.label: Study 3: random-applicant and racially and ethnically diverse-applicant human essays vs base and chain-of-thought GPT-4 essays (400 each)

assignment.what_was_assigned: No AI assistance was assigned to people. The analysis compared two groups of 400 archival human essays (random applicants and racially and ethnically diverse applicants) with 400 base GPT-4 essays and 400 chain-of-thought-prompted GPT-4 essays (p. 7, Sections 6 and 6.1).
assignment.quote: We analyzed 1,600 essays, divided equally into four groups: (1) human-written essays from random applicants, (2) human-written essays from racially and ethnically diverse applicants, (3) base GPT-4 essays, and (4) CoT-prompt GPT-4.
